doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Switching from trumpet to tuba and the step-away fingering
summary: Embouchure problems led him to switch to tuba for his recital; his relative pitch made him a step off in fingering for years.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: No. You know I played trumpet all the way through high school. I was good on trumpet. I had a scholarship to go to college, played trumpet through my first two years of college. And because of some teaching, early teaching that gave me some embouchure problems and I had to do a graduation recital in another two years, in actually a year and a half, and there was no way I would have been able to do it on trumpet so I went to a larger mouthpiece and that larger mouthpiece happened to be a tuba, and just trained new muscle rather than retraining existing muscles that had problems. And Terence Blanchard just went through this some years ago, a couple, three years ago, where he had to change his embouchure because he was having problems and it took him a while to retrain muscle. It takes, I mean to break all those habits and then come back and do it correctly,
it’s very, very difficult, and I didn’t have time to do it in that amount of time so I switched to tuba and did a recital on tuba in about a year and a half. I hated it.

You know what I mean? By that time I didn’t realize it until I switched to tuba, I started to have, not perfect, but relative pitch. I didn’t know it at the time until when I switched to tuba I found out that I could recognize all the notes on trumpet just texturally. I knew — my fingers would go down to the right place whenever the notes were played or I heard the sound, my fingers would go to the right note. And for years, I mean when I say years I mean like about ten years, I was a step away all the time playing the tuba. Because the tuba is in C and the trumpet was in B flat.

So my fingers would go to the fingering that my ear was hearing and it would always be a step away. And I got, it was so consistent I just started to trick myself and I would make myself put a finger, wrong fingering down and get the right note.
And you were a step low? Or I’m trying to figure out how that would have worked.
Well the trumpet, if I was going for a C I would go for an open note and it would be, in fact, a B flat. So I would be a step higher.
Exactly. I would be hitting the concert pitch and I would be a step higher than the note all the time.
So it was very interesting for a while.
It changes the whole harmonic scheme of the rest of the band, doesn’t it?

It certainly does. So I mean it took a while for me to really, my ear, those young ears, it’s like young kids learn languages, they hear languages much easier than people of age. And my young ears were able to get relative pitch in those first six years that I was playing trumpet.
